<p id="mntl-sc-block_2-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> Individual investors continue to prove their resilience and maintain their optimism more than halfway through a volatile year for stocks and continued geopolitical uncertainty, according to <em>Investopedia</em>‘s latest reader survey.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_3-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_4-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> Sixty percent of readers say they are optimistic or cautiously optimistic about the stock market, though many are worried about the impact of the war with Iran, which has <a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/beige-book-fed-report-glimpses-us-economic-trends-through-the-fog-of-war-12020177" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="null">driven up prices</a> throughout the economy. That level of optimism is up from 50% in April, and the highest it has been all year.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_5-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_6-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-iframe mntl-sc-block-universal-iframe mntl-block "><iframe id="mntl-sc-block-universal-iframe__uri_1-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block-universal-iframe__uri mntl-block lazyload mntl-sc-block-iframe__uri" allow="encrypted-media 'src'" data-src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/gpP7Z/1/" allowfullscreen="false" frameborder="0" title="Investors Remain Cautiously Optimistic Amid Geopolitical Fears"></iframe></div>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_7-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<span class="heading-toc" id="toc-investors-lean-toward-etfs-amid-single-stock-volatility"></span><h2 id="mntl-sc-block_8-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-heading mntl-sc-block-heading"> <span class="mntl-sc-block-heading__text text-title-300"> Investors Lean Toward ETFs Amid Single Stock Volatility </span> </h2>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_9-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> While most investors remain optimistic, their appetite for individual stocks may be waning. More than one-third of respondents indicated that they are buying more <a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/terms/e/etf.asp" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="null">exchange-traded funds</a> than stocks in recent weeks. That may be in response to heightened volatility and fears of bubbles in semiconductor and AI-related stocks like SanDisk (<a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=SNDK" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="2" rel="null">SNDK</a>) and Nvidia (<a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=NVDA" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="3" rel="null">NVDA</a>).
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_10-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_11-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> According to Vanda Research, SanDisk and Nvidia have been among the most sold stocks by individual investors outside of their retirement accounts, while SpaceX (<a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=SPCX" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="null">SPCX</a>) and Microsoft (<a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=MSFT" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="2" rel="null">MSFT</a>) are among those most purchased over the past two weeks.<span data-cite="2" class="inline-citation-node"></span><span data-cite="1" class="inline-citation-node"></span>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_12-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_13-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> While the stock market itself has traded in a fairly narrow range in 2026, individual stocks like Micron Technology (<a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=MU" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="null">MU</a>), IBM (<a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=IBM" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="2" rel="null">IBM</a>) and Western Digital (<a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=WDC" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="3" rel="null">WDC</a>) have experienced price swings of over 25% within a day or week.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_14-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_15-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-iframe mntl-sc-block-universal-iframe mntl-block "><iframe id="mntl-sc-block-universal-iframe__uri_2-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block-universal-iframe__uri mntl-block lazyload mntl-sc-block-iframe__uri" allow="encrypted-media 'src'" data-src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/M1zbh/3/" allowfullscreen="false" frameborder="0" title="More Than Half of Investors Believe AI-Related Stocks Are Overvalued"></iframe></div>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_16-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<span class="heading-toc" id="toc-mind-the-bubbles"></span><h2 id="mntl-sc-block_17-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-heading mntl-sc-block-heading"> <span class="mntl-sc-block-heading__text text-title-300"> Mind the Bubbles </span> </h2>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_18-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> More than half of respondents think that AI-related stocks are in a bubble even though many of those stocks are among their top holdings.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_19-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_20-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> FOMO, or fear of missing out, may be keeping them from selling long-held positions in stocks like Nvidia and Micron, chipmakers that have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI buildout.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_21-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_22-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> A small cohort of respondents say they have been paring back their positions in <a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/magnificent-seven-stocks-8402262" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="null">Magnificent 7</a> stocks and adding international stocks, energy stocks, index funds and ETFs.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_23-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<figure id="mntl-sc-block_24-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-image mntl-sc-block-image mntl-sc-block-image--no-theme no-theme inline-image figure-landscape figure-high-res"> <div class="figure-media">

<p id="mntl-sc-block_25-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> Investors have suffered through plenty of headline risk in 2026 amid the wars in Iran and Ukraine, tariff uncertainty and persistent inflation. Those remain among investors’ top concerns today, yet the majority of respondents are not expecting the market to drop significantly because of them. Respondents remain fairly split on whether they expect the stock market will rise or fall 5% or more over the next six months.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_26-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_27-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-iframe mntl-sc-block-universal-iframe mntl-block "><iframe id="mntl-sc-block-universal-iframe__uri_3-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block-universal-iframe__uri mntl-block lazyload mntl-sc-block-iframe__uri" allow="encrypted-media 'src'" data-src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/63Psi/1/" allowfullscreen="false" frameborder="0" title="The War In The Middle East Is The Main Concern Among Investors"></iframe></div>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_28-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<span class="heading-toc" id="toc-politics-and-markets"></span><h2 id="mntl-sc-block_29-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-heading mntl-sc-block-heading"> <span class="mntl-sc-block-heading__text text-title-300"> Politics and Markets </span> </h2>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_30-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> Most respondents like to keep their politics and their investments separate, which has been a sound strategy for decades. It may be getting harder to do that lately, as the Trump administration has made as much as <a href="https://www.csis.org/analysis/understanding-federal-equity-investments-strategic-companies" data-type="" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="noopener noreferrer">$10 billion</a> in direct equity investments in public companies like Intel (<a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=INTC" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="2" rel="null">INTC</a>) and MP Materials (<a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/markets/quote?tvwidgetsymbol=MP" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="3" rel="null">MP</a>), a rare-earth mining company, among others. More than two-thirds of respondents say they’re opposed to the government making direct investments in public companies. 
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_31-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_32-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> More than 40% of respondents approve of the Fed’s handling of interest rate policy, which is down from 57% in April before <a class="null" href="https://www.investopedia.com/5-takeaways-from-fed-chair-warsh-s-testimony-to-congress-12018900" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1" rel="null">Kevin Warsh</a> became Fed Chair. Thirty percent are concerned about the Fed’s independence, which has also dropped since Warsh took over the role.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_33-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<span class="heading-toc" id="toc-what-would-you-do-with-an-extra-10000"></span><h2 id="mntl-sc-block_34-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-heading mntl-sc-block-heading"> <span class="mntl-sc-block-heading__text text-title-300"> What Would You Do With an Extra $10,000? </span> </h2>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_35-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> Investors remain fairly split on what they would do with an extra $10,000 to invest right now, with 22% selecting ETFs and 21% selecting individual stocks. ETFs and stocks have rotated as the number one and two choices for the past year, with ETFs claiming the top spot during periods of market turbulence. Given the ongoing geopolitical uncertainty and instability, it’s not a surprise that they are investors’ top choice now. 
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_36-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>

Learn about our editorial policies Published July 16, 2026 04:58 PM EDT Many chip and AI stocks have pulled back lately amid worries about their valuations and the strength of the tech trade. Michael Nagle / Bloomberg / Getty Images Close Key Takeaways Individual investors remain cautiously optimistic about the stock market, according to Investopedia ‘s quarterly survey. Fears of bubbles in and overvaluations of AI shares persist, yet most investors are holding their positions in those stocks. Investors are favoring ETFs, energy and foreign stocks more than they did earlier this year. The impact of the war in Iran and inflation are top concerns. Get personalized, AI-powered answers built on 27+ years of trusted expertise. Ask anything to get started... ASK Individual investors continue to prove their resilience and maintain their optimism more than halfway through a volatile year for stocks and continued geopolitical uncertainty, according to Investopedia ‘s latest reader survey. Sixty percent of readers say they are optimistic or cautiously optimistic about the stock market, though many are worried about the impact of the war with Iran, which has driven up prices throughout the economy. That level of optimism is up from 50% in April, and the highest it has been all year. Investors Lean Toward ETFs Amid Single Stock Volatility While most investors remain optimistic, their appetite for individual stocks may be waning. More than one-third of respondents indicated that they are buying more exchange-traded funds than stocks in recent weeks. That may be in response to heightened volatility and fears of bubbles in semiconductor and AI-related stocks like SanDisk ( SNDK ) and Nvidia ( NVDA ). According to Vanda Research, SanDisk and Nvidia have been among the most sold stocks by individual investors outside of their retirement accounts, while SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ) are among those most purchased over the past two weeks. While the stock market itself has traded in a fairly narrow range in 2026, individual stocks like Micron Technology ( MU ), IBM ( IBM ) and Western Digital ( WDC ) have experienced price swings of over 25% within a day or week. Mind the Bubbles More than half of respondents think that AI-related stocks are in a bubble even though many of those stocks are among their top holdings. FOMO, or fear of missing out, may be keeping them from selling long-held positions in stocks like Nvidia and Micron, chipmakers that have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI buildout. A small cohort of respondents say they have been paring back their positions in Magnificent 7 stocks and adding international stocks, energy stocks, index funds and ETFs. Investors have suffered through plenty of headline risk in 2026 amid the wars in Iran and Ukraine, tariff uncertainty and persistent inflation. Those remain among investors’ top concerns today, yet the majority of respondents are not expecting the market to drop significantly because of them. Respondents remain fairly split on whether they expect the stock market will rise or fall 5% or more over the next six months. Politics and Markets Most respondents like to keep their politics and their investments separate, which has been a sound strategy for decades. It may be getting harder to do that lately, as the Trump administration has made as much as $10 billion in direct equity investments in public companies like Intel ( INTC ) and MP Materials ( MP ), a rare-earth mining company, among others. More than two-thirds of respondents say they’re opposed to the government making direct investments in public companies.  More than 40% of respondents approve of the Fed’s handling of interest rate policy, which is down from 57% in April before Kevin Warsh became Fed Chair. Thirty percent are concerned about the Fed’s independence, which has also dropped since Warsh took over the role. What Would You Do With an Extra $10,000? Investors remain fairly split on what they would do with an extra $10,000 to invest right now, with 22% selecting ETFs and 21% selecting individual stocks. ETFs and stocks have rotated as the number one and two choices for the past year, with ETFs claiming the top spot during periods of market turbulence. Given the ongoing geopolitical uncertainty and instability, it’s not a surprise that they are investors’ top choice now. Do you have a news tip for Investopedia reporters? <p id="mntl-sc-block_2-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> President Donald Trump’s promise to send every U.S. adult a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” would be the largest cash payment from the government in dollar terms in history, with a cost to rival that of the biggest federal programs.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_3-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_4-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> Speaking at a Republican midterm convention in Dallas Wednesday evening, Trump pledged to send $5,000 to every U.S. adult if Republicans retain control of both houses of Congress after November.<span data-cite="1" class="inline-citation-node"></span>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_5-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_6-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> If checks went to each of the 267 million people over 18 in the U.S., the checks would cost the government $1.35 trillion, about as much as was allocated to the military in 2026.<span data-cite="3" class="inline-citation-node"></span><span data-cite="2" class="inline-citation-node"></span> The checks would be more than triple the $1,200 COVID-19 relief checks Trump’s administration and Congress sent out in 2020 after the pandemic hit.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_7-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_8-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-iframe mntl-sc-block-universal-iframe mntl-block "><iframe id="mntl-sc-block-universal-iframe__uri_1-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block-universal-iframe__uri mntl-block lazyload mntl-sc-block-iframe__uri" allow="encrypted-media 'src'" data-src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/5Mjov/1/" allowfullscreen="false" frameborder="0" title="Reality Check"></iframe></div>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_9-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_10-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> “Because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said. “Very much like a successful company will do a cash distribution to its shareholders.”
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_11-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_12-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-callout mntl-sc-block-universal-callout theme-advisorinsight finance-sc-block-callout--generic" data-tracking-id="mntl-sc-block-callout" data-tracking-container="true"> <h3 class="mntl-sc-block-universal-callout__heading">What This Means For The Economy</h3>
<div class="mntl-sc-block-universal-callout__body"><p>While the $5,000 checks would help household budgets, critics say the move would stoke inflation and destabilize the financial system.</p></div>
<div id="finance-sc-block-callout__icon-container_1-0" class="comp finance-sc-block-callout__icon-container mntl-block"><svg class="icon finance-sc-block-callout__icon--advisor-insight "
>
<use xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#finance-sc-block-callout__icon--advisor-insight" href="#finance-sc-block-callout__icon--advisor-insight"></use>
</svg></div></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_13-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> The idea drew criticism from both sides of the political aisle. The Center for a Responsible Federal Budget, a think tank that advocates for smaller spending deficits, called it “fundamentally unserious.”
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_14-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_15-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> “Debt is now as large as our entire economy, deficits are running $2 trillion per year, inflation is about 3.5%, and the 10-year Treasury yield is approaching 5%,” CRFB president Maya MacGuinness wrote in a statement. “This half-baked political scheme would make this all worse – exploding the deficit, ginning up inflation, and further driving up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy.”
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_16-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_17-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> Vice President J.D. Vance, in an appearance on Fox News, said the checks would be paid for by the “vast amounts of revenue” generated by the tariffs Trump imposed starting in 2025. However, Import taxes added only $133 billion—about a tenth of the proposed checks—to government coffers after <a href="https://www.investopedia.com/tariff-refunds-contribute-to-record-setting-corporate-profit-boost-12068800" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1">refunding companies</a> for <a href="https://www.investopedia.com/supreme-court-strikes-down-most-of-trump-s-tariffs-11881770" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="2">tariffs deemed illegal</a> by the Supreme Court in February, the Penn-Wharton Budget Model estimated.<span data-cite="4" class="inline-citation-node"></span>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_18-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>

<p id="mntl-sc-block_21-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> The Trump Dividend is also not the only cash payment the president has promised.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_22-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_23-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> Last year, Trump said he would <a href="https://www.investopedia.com/don-t-start-spending-that-usd5000-doge-check-just-yet-musk-trump-11683618" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1">send payments equalling 20% of the savings</a> identified by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, which had set a goal of cutting government spending by $2 trillion. (In the end, DOGE found $215 billion in savings before being shut down, although the Government Accountability Office noted that much of the group’s accounting of the savings it found was “incorrect or lacked supporting evidence.”)<span data-cite="5" class="inline-citation-node"></span> Had those savings materialized, they would have resulted in $400 billion being sent to taxpayers, or about $1,500 per adult.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_24-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_25-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> Trump also promised last year to <a href="https://www.investopedia.com/trump-says-congress-doesn-t-need-to-approve-tariff-rebate-checks-experts-disagree-11889846" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1">send $2,000 “tariff rebate” checks</a> to middle and lower-class Americans. It was unclear whether the Trump Dividends replaced or added to that earlier promise, which the CRFB estimated would cost $600 billion if distributed with income criteria similar to those used for COVID-era government stimulus checks.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_26-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_27-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> Although neither of those proposals has come to fruition, Trump has also sent or promised smaller amounts of money to more limited groups of taxpayers. On Thursday, the administration said it would pay $500 each to about 1 million people on Obamacare plans, who they said had been overcharged.<span data-cite="7" class="inline-citation-node"></span> In January, the military sent $1,776 “Warrior Dividend” checks to 1.4 million service members.<span data-cite="6" class="inline-citation-node"></span>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_28-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_29-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> Should the payments be delivered as promised, they would undermine Trump’s <a href="https://www.investopedia.com/national-debt-likely-to-grow-no-matter-who-wins-us-presidential-election-8653540" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="1">repeated campaign promises</a> to pay off the national debt, <a href="https://www.investopedia.com/how-the-national-debt-affects-your-finances-today-12064710" data-component="link" data-source="inlineLink" data-type="internalLink" data-ordinal="2">which is at a record $40 trillion</a> and climbing.
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_30-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_31-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> Trump pushed back against criticism Friday in a social media post, saying the checks would be given to “all Adults in the United States.”<span data-cite="8" class="inline-citation-node"></span>
</p>
<div id="mntl-sc-block_32-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block mntl-sc-block-adslot mntl-block"></div>
<p id="mntl-sc-block_33-0" class="comp mntl-sc-block finance-sc-block-html mntl-sc-block-html"> “When I say something, I mean it! The $5,000 Dividend will happen because the People of our Country deserve it,” he wrote.<br/><br/><strong><em>Correction, Sept. 10, 2026</em></strong><em>—A previous version of this story incorrectly identified the value of the 2020 stimulus checks. </em><br/><strong><em>Update, Sept. 11, 2026—</em></strong><em>This story was updated to include President Donald Trump’s social media post. This article was originally published Sept. 10, 2026.</em>
</p>

Andrew Harnik / Getty Images Close Key Takeaways President Donald Trump promised to send $5,000 to U.S. citizens if the Republicans win the midterm elections in November. The checks would total $1.3 trillion, about the size of the U.S. military’s 2026 budget. If that and other promised cash payments were approved by Congress and sent out, the total amount would exceed the cost of any government program. Get personalized, AI-powered answers built on 27+ years of trusted expertise. Ask anything to get started... ASK President Donald Trump’s promise to send every U.S. adult a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” would be the largest cash payment from the government in dollar terms in history, with a cost to rival that of the biggest federal programs. Speaking at a Republican midterm convention in Dallas Wednesday evening, Trump pledged to send $5,000 to every U.S. adult if Republicans retain control of both houses of Congress after November. If checks went to each of the 267 million people over 18 in the U.S., the checks would cost the government $1.35 trillion, about as much as was allocated to the military in 2026. The checks would be more than triple the $1,200 COVID-19 relief checks Trump’s administration and Congress sent out in 2020 after the pandemic hit. “Because of our tremendous strength and success economically, I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said. “Very much like a successful company will do a cash distribution to its shareholders.” What This Means For The Economy While the $5,000 checks would help household budgets, critics say the move would stoke inflation and destabilize the financial system. The idea drew criticism from both sides of the political aisle. The Center for a Responsible Federal Budget, a think tank that advocates for smaller spending deficits, called it “fundamentally unserious.” “Debt is now as large as our entire economy, deficits are running $2 trillion per year, inflation is about 3.5%, and the 10-year Treasury yield is approaching 5%,” CRFB president Maya MacGuinness wrote in a statement. “This half-baked political scheme would make this all worse – exploding the deficit, ginning up inflation, and further driving up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy.” Vice President J.D. Vance, in an appearance on Fox News, said the checks would be paid for by the “vast amounts of revenue” generated by the tariffs Trump imposed starting in 2025. However, Import taxes added only $133 billion—about a tenth of the proposed checks—to government coffers after refunding companies for tariffs deemed illegal by the Supreme Court in February, the Penn-Wharton Budget Model estimated. Related Education Stimulus Checks Explained: Definition, Benefits, and Key Criticisms Understanding Helicopter Money: Examples, Types, and Economic Impact The Trump Dividend is also not the only cash payment the president has promised. Last year, Trump said he would send payments equalling 20% of the savings identified by Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, which had set a goal of cutting government spending by $2 trillion. (In the end, DOGE found $215 billion in savings before being shut down, although the Government Accountability Office noted that much of the group’s accounting of the savings it found was “incorrect or lacked supporting evidence.”) Had those savings materialized, they would have resulted in $400 billion being sent to taxpayers, or about $1,500 per adult. Trump also promised last year to send $2,000 “tariff rebate” checks to middle and lower-class Americans. It was unclear whether the Trump Dividends replaced or added to that earlier promise, which the CRFB estimated would cost $600 billion if distributed with income criteria similar to those used for COVID-era government stimulus checks. Although neither of those proposals has come to fruition, Trump has also sent or promised smaller amounts of money to more limited groups of taxpayers. On Thursday, the administration said it would pay $500 each to about 1 million people on Obamacare plans, who they said had been overcharged. In January, the military sent $1,776 “Warrior Dividend” checks to 1.4 million service members. Should the payments be delivered as promised, they would undermine Trump’s repeated campaign promises to pay off the national debt, which is at a record $40 trillion and climbing. Trump pushed back against criticism Friday in a social media post, saying the checks would be given to “all Adults in the United States.” “When I say something, I mean it! The $5,000 Dividend will happen because the People of our Country deserve it,” he wrote.
